ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: Image description: The diagram shows right triangle ABC with C at the lower left, B above C, and A to the right on the horizontal base AC. Segment BD is drawn from B to a point D on AC, and P lies on segment BD inside the triangle. Reasoning: Since ∠ACB is 90°, ∠ABC is 60°, and AB = 10, triangle ABC is a 30-60-90 triangle with hypotenuse AB. Therefore BC = 5 and AC = 5√3. Let E be the point on AC such that BE = 5√2. Because BC is perpendicular to AC, triangle BCE is right, so CE² + BC² = BE². Thus CE² + 5² = (5√2)², giving CE² = 25, so CE = 5. For any point P inside triangle ABC, extending BP meets AC at D. Since BD = √(BC² + CD²), BD increases as D moves farther from C along AC. Therefore BD > 5√2 exactly when CD > CE = 5, meaning D lies beyond E toward A. The points P with D beyond E fill triangle BEA. All possible points P fill triangle BCA. These two triangles share the same altitude from B to AC, so the probability is the ratio of their bases: area(BEA)/area(BCA) = EA/CA = (5√3 - 5)/(5√3) = (3 - √3)/3.

method.method_draft: Use polar coordinates centered at B. From the text, find BC=5 and angle ABC=60 degrees, so rays from B sweeping the triangle range from direction BC to direction BA through an angle of π/3. Let φ be the angle a ray makes with BC. Since AC is perpendicular to BC and lies 5 units below B, the distance from B to AC along that ray is L(φ)=5 sec φ. The condition BD>5√2 becomes 5 sec φ>5√2, so φ>π/4. For a uniform point P, the area swept by directions in an interval is ∫(1/2)L(φ)^2 dφ.
